subject: biology
topicDisplay: C1 — Interaction and interdependence: enzymes, respiration and photosynthesis
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Enzymes speed up reactions without being used up
Metabolism is a network of reactions, each with its own enzyme
Anabolism builds and uses energy; catabolism breaks down and releases it
Enzyme and substrate both change shape as they bind
Random motion brings substrate and active site together
Active site shape explains specificity and why denaturation stops activity
Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
Enzymes lower activation energy but not the energy released
ATP carries energy from where it is released to where it is used
What cells spend ATP on
Hydrolysing ATP releases energy; making it takes energy in
Respiration makes ATP inside cells; gas exchange is something else
Aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans compared
Measuring the rate of respiration
Carbon dioxide plus water gives glucose, with water supplying the hydrogen
Oxygen is left over from splitting water
Chromatography separates pigments, and Rf identifies them
Pigments absorb only certain wavelengths, exciting electrons
Testing how limiting factors change the rate
Growing plants in extra carbon dioxide to predict the future

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how an enzyme acts as a catalyst in a cell?
options: It increases the rate of a reaction that could occur without it, and is released unchanged.
It is converted into product along with the substrate, so the cell must keep making it.
It makes possible a reaction that could not take place at all in its absence in the cell.
It transfers energy to the substrate so that the reaction is driven forward faster.
optionWhy: Enzymes are catalysts: they increase the rate of reactions that would otherwise occur far too slowly at cell temperature, and the enzyme is not consumed, so each molecule catalyses the reaction repeatedly.
A student who treats the enzyme as a reactant picks this. In fact the enzyme is released unchanged when the product leaves the active site; it is not consumed.

A student who has only ever seen the catalysed reaction picks this. In fact the reaction can occur without the enzyme; the enzyme increases its rate, which at cell temperature is otherwise far too slow to sustain life.
A student who thinks enzymes 'help' by supplying energy picks this. In fact the enzyme lowers the activation energy; the energy for reaction comes from the substrate molecules' own kinetic energy.
questions.explain: Enzymes are catalysts: they increase the rate of reactions that would otherwise occur far too slowly at cell temperature, and the enzyme is not consumed, so each molecule catalyses the reaction repeatedly.

questions.q: Which statement best describes metabolism in a living organism?
options: The set of reactions that release energy from food molecules to keep the organism alive and active.
A series of reactions whose rate is set only by how much substrate the organism takes in from outside.
A network of interdependent enzyme-catalysed reactions, each controlled through its own enzyme.
A set of reactions catalysed by a few general-purpose enzymes that act on many substrates.
optionWhy: A student who uses the everyday meaning of metabolism picks this. In fact metabolism includes anabolic reactions such as protein synthesis and photosynthesis as well as energy-releasing catabolic ones.
A student who thinks enzymes cannot be regulated picks this. In fact cells control metabolism by controlling the synthesis and activity of specific enzymes, not just by the supply of substrate.

Metabolism is the complex network of interdependent and interacting chemical reactions in an organism. Because each reaction depends on a specific enzyme, control over metabolism can be exerted through these enzymes.
A student who thinks enzymes are all-purpose catalysts picks this. In fact enzyme specificity means each reaction needs its own enzyme, which is why organisms require many different enzymes.
questions.explain: Metabolism is the complex network of interdependent and interacting chemical reactions in an organism. Because each reaction depends on a specific enzyme, control over metabolism can be exerted through these enzymes.

questions.q: Which process is an example of anabolism?
options: The formation of glycogen from glucose monomers by condensation reactions
The oxidation of glucose in cell respiration to provide ATP for the cell
The digestion of starch in the gut into maltose and then glucose
The hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate, which releases energy
optionWhy: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones; the formation of macromolecules such as glycogen from monomers by condensation is one of the guide's named examples, along with protein synthesis and photosynthesis.

A student who classifies respiration as anabolic because it makes ATP picks this. In fact respiration oxidizes glucose to smaller molecules, so it is catabolic; ATP is the energy carrier, not a macromolecule being built.
A student who thinks digestion is anabolic because it produces useful monomers picks this. In fact digestion is hydrolysis of macromolecules into monomers, a catabolic process.
A student who thinks anabolic reactions are the ones that release energy picks this. In fact anabolic reactions require energy; hydrolysis of ATP is a breaking-down reaction that releases it.
questions.explain: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones; the formation of macromolecules such as glycogen from monomers by condensation is one of the guide's named examples, along with protein synthesis and photosynthesis.

questions.q: According to the induced-fit model, what happens when a substrate binds to the active site of an enzyme?
options: The rigid active site admits only an exactly matching substrate.
The active site closes around a substrate that keeps its shape.
The enzyme seizes the substrate and holds it without any changes.
Both the enzyme and the substrate change shape as they bind.
optionWhy: A student still using the lock-and-key model picks this. In fact the active site is not rigid: it changes shape as the substrate binds.
A student who has noticed only the enzyme's movement picks this. In fact the substrate also changes shape on binding, and that change weakens its bonds.
A student who imagines enzymes actively catching substrates picks this. In fact substrate and active site meet by random collision, and both change shape once bound.
Students should recognize that both substrate and enzyme change shape when binding occurs. The closer fit strains bonds within the substrate, which is part of how catalysis is achieved.
questions.explain: Students should recognize that both substrate and enzyme change shape when binding occurs. The closer fit strains bonds within the substrate, which is part of how catalysis is achieved.

questions.q: ATP synthase is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and cannot move freely. How do its substrates, ADP and phosphate, reach its active site?
options: They move by random molecular motion in the fluid and collide with the fixed active site.
They cannot, so an enzyme fixed in a membrane works only after being released from it.
The enzyme extends its active site out into the fluid to capture passing substrates.
They are carried to the enzyme by a directed flow of fluid in the mitochondrion.
optionWhy: Movement is needed for a substrate and an active site to come together, but movement of the substrate alone is enough. Enzymes immobilized in membranes are reached by substrates moving randomly.
A student who thinks both partners must move picks this. In fact substrate molecules moving randomly collide with the active site of an immobilized enzyme, which works normally.
A student who imagines enzymes reaching for substrates picks this. In fact enzymes do not seek substrates; collisions arise from random molecular motion.
A student who thinks molecules stay still unless carried picks this. In fact molecules in a fluid are in constant random motion, which alone brings them into collision with the active site.
questions.explain: Movement is needed for a substrate and an active site to come together, but movement of the substrate alone is enough. Enzymes immobilized in membranes are reached by substrates moving randomly.

questions.q: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured?
options: Its peptide bonds are broken, so the polypeptide chain splits into its separate amino acids.
Its shape alters only briefly and then returns to normal once the conditions are restored.
Its three-dimensional structure changes, so the active site no longer fits the substrate.
It is killed, because enzymes are living particles that are destroyed by heat or acid.
optionWhy: A student who thinks denaturation destroys the molecule picks this. In fact the peptide bonds and primary structure remain intact; only the folding changes.
A student who extends the reversibility of low temperature to denaturation picks this. In fact denaturation is usually permanent; the enzyme does not refold correctly.

Denaturation disrupts the hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and other interactions that hold the enzyme's folded shape. The active site loses the shape and properties needed to bind the substrate, so activity is lost.
A student who takes 'killed' literally picks this. In fact enzymes are protein molecules, not living things; heat or extreme pH changes their shape.
questions.explain: Denaturation disrupts the hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and other interactions that hold the enzyme's folded shape. The active site loses the shape and properties needed to bind the substrate, so activity is lost.

questions.q: At high substrate concentrations, the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction levels off even when more substrate is added. Why?
options: Every active site is occupied almost all the time, so extra substrate finds no free site to bind.
The enzyme molecules have been used up by the reaction, so no more product can be formed.
The high concentration of substrate denatures the enzyme, so its active site stops working.
The amount of energy the enzyme can supply each second has reached its upper limit.
optionWhy: At saturation the enzyme is working at its maximum rate: as soon as one product leaves an active site another substrate binds. Adding substrate cannot increase the frequency of productive collisions further.
A student who thinks enzymes are consumed picks this. In fact enzymes are released unchanged; the plateau reflects saturation of active sites, not loss of enzyme.
A student who assumes substrate has a damaging limit like temperature picks this. In fact substrate concentration does not change the enzyme's structure.
A student who thinks enzymes supply energy picks this. In fact enzymes supply no energy; the limit is the number of active sites available for substrate to bind.
questions.explain: At saturation the enzyme is working at its maximum rate: as soon as one product leaves an active site another substrate binds. Adding substrate cannot increase the frequency of productive collisions further.

questions.q: How does an enzyme affect the energy changes of the reaction it catalyses?
options: It lowers the energy of the products, so that more energy is released overall than would be without the enzyme.
It lowers the activation energy but leaves the energy difference between substrate and products unchanged.
It supplies the activation energy, transferring its own energy to the substrate to break the bonds.
It releases energy by breaking bonds in the substrate, and this provides the activation energy.
optionWhy: A student who reads the lower catalysed curve as lower energy throughout picks this. In fact only the peak is lowered; substrate and products are at the same levels with or without the enzyme.

Energy is required to break bonds within the substrate, and the enzyme reduces this activation energy. The energy yield when bonds form in the products is a property of the reaction and is not changed.
A student who thinks the enzyme is an energy source picks this. In fact the enzyme supplies no energy; it lowers the barrier so that more substrate molecules already have enough energy to react.
A student who thinks bond breaking releases energy picks this. In fact energy is required to break bonds; energy is released when the bonds of the products are made.
questions.explain: Energy is required to break bonds within the substrate, and the enzyme reduces this activation energy. The energy yield when bonds form in the products is a property of the reaction and is not changed.

questions.q: Which statement about ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is correct?
options: It is a nucleotide: adenine and ribose joined to a chain of three phosphate groups.
It is a small protein that binds energy released from glucose in respiration.
It is the cell's main long-term reserve of energy, built up like glycogen.
It is destroyed once used and is rebuilt from glucose rather than from ADP.
optionWhy: ATP is a nucleotide made of the base adenine, the pentose sugar ribose and three phosphate groups. It is the molecule that distributes energy within cells.

A student who files nucleotides under DNA only and thinks of ATP as a special protein picks this. In fact ATP is a nucleotide, not a protein, and energy is not 'bound' but released when ATP is hydrolysed.
A student who reads 'energy store' as a reserve for the future picks this. In fact a cell holds only a small pool of ATP and recycles it within seconds; long-term reserves are glycogen and lipid.
A student who pictures each ATP being made afresh from glucose picks this. In fact hydrolysis gives ADP and phosphate, and these are rejoined to re-form ATP; glucose supplies the energy, not the ADP.
questions.explain: ATP is a nucleotide made of the base adenine, the pentose sugar ribose and three phosphate groups. It is the molecule that distributes energy within cells.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a life process that ATP supplies with energy?
options: Water entering a root hair cell by osmosis uses ATP to cross the membrane against its gradient.
Joining amino acids into a polypeptide releases energy, which the cell holds as ATP.
Pumping sodium ions out of a neuron against their concentration gradient uses ATP directly.
Chromosomes move to the poles in mitosis without ATP, pulled by spindle fibres as they get shorter.
optionWhy: A student who thinks every movement across a membrane needs ATP picks this. In fact osmosis is passive: water moves down its own gradient with no ATP hydrolysed.
A student who thinks bond-forming synthesis releases energy picks this. In fact synthesis of macromolecules (anabolism) requires energy, which ATP supplies; it does not produce ATP.
Active transport across membranes is one of the principal uses of ATP: the sodium-potassium pump hydrolyses ATP to move ions against their concentration gradients.
A student who reads mitosis diagrams as purely mechanical picks this. In fact movement of cell components such as chromosomes is driven by motor proteins that use energy from ATP.
questions.explain: Active transport across membranes is one of the principal uses of ATP: the sodium-potassium pump hydrolyses ATP to move ions against their concentration gradients.

questions.q: During a sprint, ATP in muscle fibres is hydrolysed and then re-formed thousands of times. Which statement about the energy transfers is correct?
options: Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate needs an input of energy, and re-forming ATP releases it.
Hydrolysed ATP cannot be re-formed, so each contraction needs new ATP built from a glucose molecule.
The muscle takes energy directly from glucose during the sprint; hydrolysis of ATP is a minor side reaction.
Hydrolysis of ATP releases energy; energy from respiration is needed to re-form it from ADP.
optionWhy: A student who merges 'respiration releases energy' with 'respiration makes ATP' reverses the direction and picks this. In fact energy is released by hydrolysis and required for synthesis.
A student who thinks ATP is consumed and replaced from scratch picks this. In fact the ADP and phosphate are rejoined; the same ADP molecules are recycled thousands of times during the sprint.

A student who remembers 'glucose releases energy for the cell' without ATP picks this. In fact contraction is powered by ATP hydrolysis; glucose supplies energy only through the ATP it is used to make.
Energy is released by hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate, and energy released from carbon compounds in respiration is required to synthesize ATP again from ADP and phosphate.
questions.explain: Energy is released by hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate, and energy released from carbon compounds in respiration is required to synthesize ATP again from ADP and phosphate.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the substrates of cell respiration?
options: Only glucose can be respired, because it is the reactant in the equation for respiration.
Glucose and fatty acids are the main substrates, but many other carbon compounds can be used.
Glucose and fatty acids are the substrates, and either can be used with or without oxygen.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide are the substrates, since they are the substances exchanged at the lungs.
optionWhy: A student who takes the glucose word equation as the definition of respiration picks this. In fact glucose is the standard example; a wide range of carbon compounds can be respired.
Glucose and fatty acids are the principal substrates for cell respiration, but a wide range of carbon (organic) compounds, including other sugars, glycerol and amino acids, can be respired.
A student who keeps substrates and oxygen requirement as separate lists picks this. In fact fatty acids can be respired only aerobically; only carbohydrate can be used anaerobically.

A student who confuses respiration with gas exchange picks the gases as substrates. In fact the substrate is a carbon compound; oxygen is a reactant in aerobic respiration but is not the source of the energy.
questions.explain: Glucose and fatty acids are the principal substrates for cell respiration, but a wide range of carbon (organic) compounds, including other sugars, glycerol and amino acids, can be respired.

questions.q: Which statement about anaerobic cell respiration in humans is correct?
options: Glucose is converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide, as it is in yeast cells.
Glucose is converted to lactate and carbon dioxide in the cytoplasm of the cell.
Glucose is converted to lactate, and no carbon dioxide is released at all.
Glucose is converted to lactate using a little oxygen rather than none.
optionWhy: A student who confuses the human and yeast equations picks this. In fact humans convert glucose to lactate; ethanol and carbon dioxide are the products in yeast.
A student who thinks all respiration releases carbon dioxide picks this. In fact no carbon dioxide is released in human anaerobic respiration; the only product is lactate.
The word equation is glucose → lactate. Anaerobic respiration in humans uses no oxygen, occurs in the cytoplasm, yields a little ATP and releases no carbon dioxide.

A student who reads 'anaerobic' as 'low oxygen' picks this. In fact anaerobic respiration uses no oxygen at all; it consists only of glycolysis and lactate formation in the cytoplasm, so the oxygen-using reactions in the mitochondria play no part.
questions.explain: The word equation is glucose → lactate. Anaerobic respiration in humans uses no oxygen, occurs in the cytoplasm, yields a little ATP and releases no carbon dioxide.

questions.q: In a respirometer, carbon dioxide is absorbed by potassium hydroxide. With 5.0 g of germinating seeds, the gas volume in the apparatus fell by 1.2 cm³ in 10 minutes. What is the rate of respiration per gram?
options: 0.024 cm³ of carbon dioxide produced per gram per minute
0.024 cm³ of oxygen taken up per gram per minute
0.12 cm³ of oxygen taken up per gram per minute
0.024 cm³ of oxygen given out per gram per minute
optionWhy: A student who thinks the liquid is moved by carbon dioxide picks this. In fact the potassium hydroxide absorbs the carbon dioxide, so the volume change measures oxygen uptake.
The fall in volume equals the oxygen consumed, because carbon dioxide is removed by the alkali. Rate = 1.2 cm³ ÷ 10 min ÷ 5.0 g = 0.024 cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹.
A student who divides by time but forgets to divide by the mass of seeds picks this. 1.2 ÷ 10 = 0.12 cm³ min⁻¹ for the whole 5.0 g sample; per gram this is 0.024.
A student who thinks plant material releases oxygen picks this. In fact germinating seeds respire and do not photosynthesize; the volume fell because oxygen was taken up, not released.
questions.explain: The fall in volume equals the oxygen consumed, because carbon dioxide is removed by the alkali. Rate = 1.2 cm³ ÷ 10 min ÷ 5.0 g = 0.024 cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹.

questions.q: Which word equation correctly summarises photosynthesis?
options: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
carbon dioxide + light energy → glucose + oxygen
carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
soil minerals + water → glucose + oxygen
optionWhy: A student who treats photosynthesis and respiration as interchangeable mirror images picks this. This is the summary of cell respiration, which releases the energy stored by photosynthesis.
A student who does not see water as a reactant picks this. Glucose contains hydrogen, which carbon dioxide cannot supply; the hydrogen comes from water, which is split in photosynthesis.
Carbon dioxide is converted to glucose using hydrogen obtained by splitting water, and the oxygen left over from the water is released as a by-product.
A student who thinks a plant's food is built from what its roots absorb picks this. In fact the carbon in glucose comes from carbon dioxide taken in from the air, not from soil minerals.
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide is converted to glucose using hydrogen obtained by splitting water, and the oxygen left over from the water is released as a by-product.

questions.q: Which list includes all of the groups of organisms that release oxygen as a by-product of photosynthesis?
options: Plants, algae, cyanobacteria, fungi
Plants, algae and cyanobacteria
Plants and algae, no bacteria
Land plants and no other group
optionWhy: A student who thinks of fungi as plants picks this. Fungi have no photosynthetic pigments and obtain carbon compounds by absorbing them; they release no oxygen.
Oxygen is a by-product of photosynthesis in plants, algae and cyanobacteria. Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes, but they split water in the same way and release oxygen.
A student who has only met bacteria as decomposers or pathogens picks this. Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic bacteria that split water and release oxygen.

A student who associates photosynthesis only with green plants picks this. Algae and cyanobacteria also photosynthesize and release oxygen; most of the oxygen in the atmosphere first came from cyanobacteria.
questions.explain: Oxygen is a by-product of photosynthesis in plants, algae and cyanobacteria. Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes, but they split water in the same way and release oxygen.

questions.q: On a paper chromatogram of leaf pigments, the origin line was 20 mm from the bottom edge of the paper, the centre of the carotene spot was 65 mm from the bottom edge and the solvent front was 70 mm from the bottom edge. What is the Rf value of carotene?
optionWhy: A student who measures from the bottom edge of the paper instead of the origin line divides 65 by 70. Both distances must be measured from the origin, giving 45 ÷ 50.
A student who puts the solvent distance on top divides 50 by 45. Rf is the pigment distance divided by the solvent distance and can never exceed 1.
Both distances are measured from the origin: the pigment moved 65 − 20 = 45 mm and the solvent front moved 70 − 20 = 50 mm. Rf = 45 ÷ 50 = 0.90.

A student who measures the gap between the spot and the solvent front (5 mm) instead of the distance from the origin picks this. The pigment travelled 45 mm from the origin, so the Rf is high, not low.
questions.explain: Both distances are measured from the origin: the pigment moved 65 − 20 = 45 mm and the solvent front moved 70 − 20 = 50 mm. Rf = 45 ÷ 50 = 0.90.

questions.q: A chlorophyll molecule in a leaf absorbs a photon of red light. What happens within the molecule as a result?
options: An electron is raised to a higher energy level.
It vibrates faster, warming the surrounding stroma.
It splits a molecule of water that is bound to it.
It stores the light inside itself until it is needed.
optionWhy: Absorbing a photon excites an electron within the pigment molecule, raising it to a higher energy level. This is the step in which light energy is transformed into chemical energy, carried by the excited electron.
A student who thinks light is used as heat picks this. The absorbed energy goes into exciting an electron, not into heating; the excited electron's energy is what photosynthesis captures.

A student who takes 'photolysis' to mean that light splits water directly picks this. Absorption excites an electron; water is split by photosystem II only after the reaction centre has lost an electron.
A student who thinks plants store sunlight picks this. Light cannot be stored; its energy is transformed at once into the energy of an excited electron and then into chemical energy.
questions.explain: Absorbing a photon excites an electron within the pigment molecule, raising it to a higher energy level. This is the step in which light energy is transformed into chemical energy, carried by the excited electron.

questions.q: A student places a lamp at different distances from a beaker of pondweed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution kept at 25 °C, and counts the bubbles of gas released per minute at each distance. Which correctly identifies the variables?
options: Independent: lamp distance; dependent: bubbles per minute
Independent: bubbles per minute; dependent: distance of lamp
Controlled variable: lamp distance; dependent: bubbles per minute
Independent: temperature of 25 °C; dependent: bubbles per minute
optionWhy: The lamp distance is what the student deliberately changes (it sets the light intensity), so it is the independent variable; the bubble count is measured to find the effect, so it is the dependent variable. Temperature and hydrogencarbonate concentration are controlled variables.

A student who reasons that the result 'depends on' the light and so calls the light dependent picks this. The independent variable is the one the investigator changes; the dependent variable is the one measured.

A student who thinks 'controlled' means 'set by the experimenter' picks this. The lamp distance is varied, so it is the independent variable; controlled variables are those held constant, such as temperature.

A student who picks the variable with a fixed number attached picks this. Temperature is kept constant, so it is a controlled variable; the independent variable is the one that changes between trials, the lamp distance.
questions.explain: The lamp distance is what the student deliberately changes (it sets the light intensity), so it is the independent variable; the bubble count is measured to find the effect, so it is the dependent variable. Temperature and hydrogencarbonate concentration are controlled variables.

questions.q: Tomato plants were grown in two enclosed greenhouses, one at 400 ppm carbon dioxide and one at 800 ppm. Both were kept at 22 °C with the same lighting and watering, and after six weeks the dry mass of the plants was measured. Which is a controlled variable in this experiment?
options: The carbon dioxide concentration in the greenhouses
The dry mass of the plants measured at six weeks
The plants grown at 400 ppm carbon dioxide
The temperature of 22 °C in both greenhouses
optionWhy: A student who thinks the controlled variable is the one the experimenter sets picks this. Carbon dioxide concentration is deliberately varied between the greenhouses, so it is the independent variable.

A student who thinks 'controlled' means 'carefully measured' picks this. Dry mass is what is measured to find the effect of the carbon dioxide, so it is the dependent variable; controlled variables are those held constant.

A student who merges 'control' with 'controlled variable' picks this. The plants at 400 ppm are the control treatment for comparison; a controlled variable is a factor held constant, such as temperature.

Temperature could affect growth, so it is kept the same in both greenhouses to ensure that any difference in dry mass is due to carbon dioxide alone. That makes it a controlled variable; lighting and watering are also controlled.
questions.explain: Temperature could affect growth, so it is kept the same in both greenhouses to ensure that any difference in dry mass is due to carbon dioxide alone. That makes it a controlled variable; lighting and watering are also controlled.
